With NASA's new electromagnetic resonance drive, what is being resonated? What other materials or phenomena share the resonance frequency with what is being produced inside the cavity?

First of all, we need to say that the EMDrive tests aren't officially confirmed by NASA - just by one NASA employee.

Coming back to the original question - the short answer is - nobody knows.

There have been many experiments, and they seem to show measurable thrust which can not be yet explained. The results still aren't significant enough to exclude measurement errors as a source of perceived thrust. There is no theory explaining it which could be consistent with our physics, and all other theoretical explanations either require a major rewrite of our physics, or are simply flawed.

Right now we need to more measurements - either to exclude possible error sources (if it really works) or to figure out the source of measurement errors (if it's a fluke).

There's a great deal of mortal-accessible information on the emdrive wiki - http://emdrive.wiki/Main_Page - check out possible error sources.

I understand the great potential for experimental error. However, I'm looking for ways it could be correct. For example, is there some way to make the vacuum chamber inside the drive so electrically similar to some outside force or phenomena that the resonance produces a propellant force?

Asking how this could be possible is very different than the equally important job of asking how and why it is wrong.

The big elephant in the room is that if the EMDrive works, it breaks the conservation of momentum - so without a really damn solid theory no physicist who wants to continue his/her academic life is going to touch this topic. As far as I remember, theories by mr Shawyer and Fetta (authors of EM Drive and similar Cannae drive) have been found inconsistent.

Don't get me wrong - these results are very unusual, and if they are somehow confirmed, it will be one of the most profound discoveries of humanity. I deeply wish for such outcome to come true... but until we get an undeniable experimental proof (a full scale test in space for example), or a peer reviewed theoretical explanation, I'm would not advise getting too excited. I already have been disappointed a few times (for example by supposedly superluminal neutrinos).
